title: Krishna Slays Dantavakra and Viduratha
story:
Krishna was on the road home from the war with Shalva, the dust of one victory still settling, when the road began to shake — and the men who rode with him looked up to see a single figure approaching on foot.

It was a lonely stretch of road, Dwaraka's walls still a day's march ahead, and no one on it but the returning war-party and the single figure coming to meet them. It was Dantavakra, kin to the slain Shishupala and friend to the slain Shalva, and he had not come to talk. The news of both deaths had reached his kingdom of Karusha, and he had taken up his mace and walked out to settle the debt himself — alone, on foot, the grudge in his hand.

Krishna saw him coming and knew what the day would be. He took up his own mace, Kaumodaki, and waited.

Dantavakra came on, and the ground trembled under his steps. Rage had made him careless of everything — no chariot, no army, no counsel, only the mace and the debt. He was one of those warriors the world had learned to fear, the sort of man who settles his friendships with a weapon, and the weapon he carried had never once failed him. When he was close enough to be heard, he raised it and shouted at Krishna.

'You are our own cousin, Krishna,' he called, 'and yet you turn on your own kin! You are the betrayer of friends. You killed Shishupala at his own kinsmen's sacrifice; you killed Shalva in the ruin of his city. Do you think I will let that stand? I owe my friends a debt, and I am kind to my friends — I have come to pay it with your head.'

His words were harsh as goads on an elephant, the text says, and Krishna heard them all without a word. Dantavakra came within reach, and for a moment the two stood facing each other — the mace-man and the chariot-lord — while the dust settled around them. Then Dantavakra swung.

The mace came down on Krishna's head with all the strength of that huge body behind it — a blow that would have felled a fortress wall. Krishna did not move. The Bhagavata is exact about it: struck by the mace in the very press of the fight, he did not stir, as though the blow had fallen on a mountain.

And then Kaumodaki answered. Krishna's mace struck Dantavakra square in the chest and crushed it. The king of Karusha staggered, blood pouring from his mouth, and fell — and as he fell, those who watched saw a wonder: a subtle light rose out of him and entered Krishna, a thing too fine for the eye to hold, and gone before anyone could say what it was.

Before the field could take breath, Viduratha came rushing onto the road — Dantavakra's brother, his heart drowned in grief for the brother he had just lost. He had no plan and no weapon to match the moment, only rage and sorrow. Krishna met him with the discus, razor-edged, and took his crowned head.

The road was quiet. Two brothers lay where they had fallen, and the vengeance they had come to take had ended the way vengeance usually does — in two graves instead of one. The men who rode with Krishna gathered in silence, and no one spoke of victory. They would speak for years, though, of the light they had seen leave the fallen king, uncertain of what they had witnessed.

Then Krishna turned his chariot toward Dwaraka, and the dust settled behind him.
reflection: The text passes over the violence to dwell on one detail: a subtle light leaving Dantavakra and entering Krishna. It is the strangest moment in the scene, and the most tender — the enemy who had walked out to kill his cousin returning, at the last, into the one he fought, as if the long feud had been a homecoming all along.
content_note: Mild violence: Dantavakra's chest is crushed and Viduratha is beheaded; described without gore.
next_story_tease: Far away in Hastinapura, a game of dice was about to put a queen in the hands of her enemies.
hero_scene: Struck on the head by Dantavakra's mace, Krishna stands unshaken on the road, his own mace Kaumodaki crashing into Dantavakra's chest as a subtle light streams from the falling king into Krishna, while Viduratha rushes in behind.
